title: From Death-Row Lawyer to Comedy: The Journey of Josh Pickar
seoTitle: From Death-Row Lawyer to Comedy: Josh Pickar's Journey
subtitle: After years defending inmates on death row, he uses humor to break the distance of the death penalty.
excerpt: On August 4, 2026, the former death-row lawyer reveals how stand-up and art helped him humanize the condemned and keep the death-penalty debate alive.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
On August 4, 2026, Josh Pickar, who spent seven years as a lawyer for inmates on death row in Alabama and the federal system, explains how humor became his tool to keep the debate on capital punishment active. The transition from legal practice to stand-up revealed, for him, an unexpected path of engagement and empathy.

The Misleading Video Case and the Perception of Injustice

In his early pro bono work, Pickar examined a crucial piece of evidence: a 30-second surveillance video that, when he analyzed it frame by frame, he realized it was not a continuous film but a sequence of photos presented as footage. The gaps unconsciously filled by jurors revealed an extremely deceptive governmental practice, sparking in him a strong sense of injustice and keeping him attached to the case.

Humor as a Bridge with the Condemned

During visits to inmates, the lawyer encountered unexpected moments of humor. In one meeting, a Black client in his mid-thirties, dressed in a khaki jumpsuit, laughed as he compared life on death row to that of a slain Libyan dictator. Another inmate, after receiving a yoga flyer from an officer, wrote “NOT WORKING! :P” in bold letters, showing that even in desperation, humor still emerged. These moments showed Pickar that getting to know the people behind the sentences made it harder to abstract the penal system as it usually does.

Art and Creativity Inside Prison

One of his former clients, kept in solitary confinement for decades, developed a unique artistic output. He creates abstract, distorted figures called “Sassy Boys,” adorned with tiny hats, canes, and earrings, always late and carefree. Observing this creativity, Pickar felt the humanity of the inmates became even more impossible to ignore.

From Law Practice to Stand-up: The Search for Immediacy

When he began his career as a comedian and improviser in New York, Pickar found in comedy the speed that contrasted with the sluggishness of the courts. While a judge may take months to decide an appeal, an audience can reject a joke in a single breath. This instantaneity gave him a space where the risk was lower, but the connection with the audience more direct.

How Comedy Keeps the Death-Penalty Debate Alive

Inspired by Bryan Stevenson’s “Just Mercy,” Pickar began weaving jokes about the death penalty into his shows, not to soften the topic but to prevent discomfort from making the audience tune out. He reports that even in noisy rooms, people stay attentive; after performances, questions arise about cases and the criminal-justice system itself, showing that laughter does not trivialize but sustains interest.

New Projects: Musical and Edinburgh Festival Debut

Recently, the client who creates the “Sassy Boys” called suggesting the production of a musical, just for fun. This proposal culminated in the debut of Josh Pickar’s show “Getting Off,” scheduled to take place at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, at the Assembly Roxy (Snug), from August 5 to 30. The initiative demonstrates how art, humor, and legal experience can converge into new forms of expression.

With information from The Guardian.
